fetched_contents.text: The 11- and 22- Year Cycles in Cosmic-Ray Modulation and Their Connection with the Solar Activity Abstract The observed 11- and 22-year cycles in galactic cosmic ray intensities are discussed in relation to the corresponding solar activity cycles. Yearly averaged ionization chamber data, seasonally averaged neutron monitor data and daily stratospheric gas-discharge counter data is presented which spans the period 1935 to 1980 and cut-off rigidities from 0.6 to 6.7 GV in the Northern Hemisphere and 0.02 in the Southern Hemisphere. The observed changes in cosmic ray intensity are found to be in satisfactory agreement with those calculated from the number of sunspot groups and their average heliolatitude for all years except the intervals of solar polar magnetic field reversal. Experimental intensities are noted to be less than calculated intensities during the transition from a solar magnetic moment parallel to the angular momentum to one antiparallel to the angular momentum, and to be greater than the calculated values during the opposite transition, demonstrating the dependence of galactic cosmic ray intensity on heliospheric magnetic field direction. fetched_contents.text: Atmospheric Ionizations by Solar X‐Rays, Solar Protons, and Radiation Belt Electrons in September 2017 Space Weather Event - Murase - 2023 - Space Weather 1 Introduction Atmospheric ionization is one of the most promising factors to link space weather events and terrestrial climate. For example, solar proton events can cause large-scale ozone destructions in the polar cap regions via the NOx and HOx productions by the stratospheric ionization (e.g., Jackman et al., 1993; López-Puertas et al., 2005). Recently, small-scale ozone destruction has also been identified during isolated proton aurora events via the precipitation of radiation belt electrons to the mesosphere (Ozaki et al., 2022). X-rays from solar flares and radiation belt electrons are also the ionization source of the mesosphere (e.g., Enell et al., 2008; Frahm et al., 1997). However, the relative importance of X-ray radiation from solar flares, precipitation of solar protons, and radiation belt electrons in the transient ionization of the middle atmosphere has been poorly discussed in the literature. It is because those phenomena occur in different regions at different temporal scales and that many studies have been focusing on only one aspect or two (e.g., Bailey, 1959; Beharrell et al., 2015; Curto, 2020; Thorne, 1980; Verronen et al., 2015; Webber, 1962). As a good review combining many of such studies, for instance, Mironova et al. (2015) summarized the possible ranges of ionization rates of different sources. One of the purposes of this study is to examine it, focusing on the latest space weather event. The September 2017 space weather event was one of the most active periods in the solar cycle 24. Broad ranges of causes and effects have been discussed in previous studies, for example, in terms of solar energetic particles and their impact on the ionosphere and atmosphere from low to high latitudes (Bruno et al., 2019; O’Brien et al., 2018; Pikulina et al., 2022; Qian et al., 2019 and reference therein). Especially in the auroral region, they have discussed all of the penetration of solar protons into the polar cap region, solar X-rays in the daytime, and the precipitation of radiation belt electrons due to active geomagnetic activity. Note that the observations of atmospheric ionization due to these precipitations have been recognized as essential for diagnosing and quantifying the energy input to the atmosphere by energetic particles. Yamauchi et al. (2018) summarized ionospheric responses in the Arctic region with the observations of the European Incoherent SCATter (EISCAT) radars during 6–8 September 2017. They showed the enhancements of the electron density during the periods of two X-class flares and a solar proton event on 6 and 7 September, respectively, while the quantitative connections were not made between the energy input of energetic particles and the resultant electron density variations. In this study, we address the quantitative understanding of the ionization profiles during September 2017 event, utilizing a Monte Carlo simulation of particle transport and cutting-edge ground-based and space-borne observations. More specifically, we quantitatively examine the relative importance and possible errors of all the different types of ionizations and discuss the cause of errors and limitations of our methods. In Section 2, we briefly describe the data sets of the observations and simulation. The observational data and quantitative examination via the air-shower simulation are shown in Section 3, and the discussion follows in Section 4. Concluding remarks are summarized in Section 5. 2 Data Sets 2.1 Ground-Based Observations The PANSY radar, the Program of the Antarctic Syowa Mesosphere–Stratosphere–Troposphere/Incoherent Scatter radar, is located at Syowa Station in the Antarctic region (69.0S, 39.6E; CGMLAT = −66.5°). The radar has been in full and continuous operation since October 2015. The observation frequency is 47 MHz with five beams in the directions of the local zenith, geographic north, east, south, and west with zenith angles of 10°. The range resolution in the mesospheric observation at 40–100 km altitude is 600 m in winter, and these data are obtained every ∼4 min (Sato et al., 2014). We used the altitude-resolved mesospheric echo power as a proxy for the increase in the electron density (Kataoka et al., 2019; Murase et al., 2022; Nishiyama et al., 2015; Tanaka et al., 2019). Syowa Station is a manned comprehensive geophysical observatory, where several different observations are also conducted for geophysical studies. The most relevant to this study is the imaging riometer. The imaging riometer measures cosmic noise absorption (CNA) sensitive to the precipitation of electrons of several tens to several hundreds of keV. The imaging array consists of 8 × 8 beams, covering an area of 180 km × 180 km at 80 km altitude. The observation frequency of the imaging riometer is 38.2 MHz, with an angular resolution of ∼10° near the zenith. The data sampling interval is 1 s. The EISCAT radars, European Incoherent Scatter radars, have been operated in Northern Scandinavia since 1981 and Svalbard since 1996. During X-class solar flares on September 6, the electron density in the ionosphere was also observed by the EISCAT VHF radar at Tromsø (69.6N, 19.2E; CGMLAT = 66.7°) with the observation frequency of 224 MHz. The VHF radar pointed at geographic north at a low elevation angle of 30°. We used electron density data derived from one-minute integration in this study to improve the accuracy of the electron density derivation at low altitudes (below 80 km). Physical mechanisms driving stratospheric ionization rate variations are rooted in a combination of direct ionization sources and loss processes that reduce net ionization. The primary ionization sources identified in the evidence are solar UV, X-rays, and cosmic rays. The cited material describes galactic cosmic-ray energy deposition and its implications for stratospheric chemistry, and another source explicitly notes that cosmic rays drive electron-induced reactions and ozone depletion [N1-R2][N1-R4][N1-R5]. It also emphasizes that electrons are produced by photoionization of atoms with ionization potentials below 13.6 eV, indicating that solar UV and X-ray photoionization are central to ion production in the atmosphere [N1-R3]. This supports the idea that solar UV/X-ray ionization is the dominant daytime source of stratospheric electrons.

Particle precipitation and auroral electrons are additional contributors, especially in polar and auroral regions. The cited studies on stratospheric ionization by solar X-rays, solar protons, and radiation belt electrons show that energetic particles can penetrate the atmosphere and generate ionization, while the auroral region is highlighted as a site where particle precipitation and electron fluxes are important for ionization and ozone destruction [N4-F1][N2-R4]. The auroral zone and polar regions are especially significant because particle precipitation is not uniform across latitude; auroral electrons and precipitating protons can enhance ionization there [N3-R2][N3-R5]. These precipitation events are physically tied to magnetic-field geometry, as the evidence indicates that auroral particle precipitation is part of a coupled electrodynamical system involving field-aligned currents and precipitating particles [N3-R3].

A critical counteracting effect is electron attachment and recombination, which reduce net ionization. The evidence explicitly states that electron scavengers like sulfur hexafluoride can attach electrons to form stable negative ions, and that the loss rate of electrons is slow enough for the ionosphere to persist through the night at higher altitudes [N5-R3][N4-F2]. This implies that electron attachment lowers the effective ionization rate by removing free electrons before they can sustain further ionization processes. In the context of stratospheric ionization, this means that even if primary ionization sources are strong, the net ionization rate depends on how many electrons are retained versus lost to attachment and recombination [N1-R5][N5-R3].

Overall, the variation in ionization rates is therefore driven by: solar UV/X-ray photoionization, cosmic-ray-induced electron production, auroral and polar particle precipitation, and the competing loss of electrons through attachment and recombination [N1-R2][N1-R3][N4-F1][N5-R3].

The evidence highlights that cosmic-ray-driven electron-induced reactions are linked to ozone depletion, and that electron attachment can suppress ozone destruction [N5-R1][N5-R3]. This indicates a direct feedback: ionization can alter the availability of electrons that participate in ozone chemistry, and electron scavengers reduce the magnitude of ozone-depleting reactions [N5-R3]. The cited study on stratospheric chemistry also notes that cosmic-ray energy deposition has implications for atmospheric chemistry, further supporting the idea that ionization is not an isolated process but part of a broader chemical network [N1-R2].

Aerosol and radical production are also influenced by ionization, although the evidence here is more indirect. The electron-induced reaction mechanism is described as relevant to global ozone depletion, which is a key pathway for radical chemistry and subsequent ozone chemistry, but the provided citations do not explicitly detail aerosol production from ionization [N1-R1][N5-R1]. Still, the fact that ionization can enhance or suppress ozone-depleting reactions implies that it can affect the broader oxidizing environment in which aerosol precursors and radicals form [N5-R3]. The evidence also points to electron attachment lowering ozone destruction, which indirectly supports the idea that ionization can change the balance between oxidants and reductants in the atmosphere [N5-R3].

Relevance to atmospheric dynamics and radiative forcing is more suggestive than definitive in the provided evidence. The cited material on the Earth’s ionosphere notes that ionospheric charged particles result from ionization and are affected by gravity and electromagnetic forces, and that gravitational and electromagnetic forces contribute to ionospheric characteristics [N4-F2]. While this is more about the ionosphere than the stratosphere, it illustrates that ionization is embedded in a larger dynamical and electrical system. The evidence also links ionization to ozone and chemistry, which are themselves important for radiative forcing because ozone absorbs solar radiation and affects surface temperatures [N4-F2]. Therefore, even though the provided material does not directly quantify radiative forcing, it supports the conclusion that ionization variations can affect chemistry, which in turn influences dynamics and climate [N4-F2][N5-R3].

## Integrated explanation of stratospheric ionization rate variations by geomagnetic latitude and solar activity

The variations in stratospheric ionization rates are caused by a combination of direct ionization sources, loss processes, and the way those processes are modulated by solar activity and geomagnetic latitude. The evidence points to three main drivers: solar UV/X-ray photoionization and cosmic-ray-induced electron production as primary sources of ionization; particle precipitation and auroral electrons as additional contributors in polar and auroral regions; and electron attachment and recombination as loss processes that reduce net ionization [N1-R2][N1-R3][N5-R3][N4-F1].

## 1) Primary ionization sources and how they vary with altitude and source type

The most direct ionization sources are solar UV and X-rays, which photoionize atmospheric atoms and molecules, and cosmic rays, which drive electron production and subsequent ionization. The evidence states that cosmic-ray energy deposition and related ionization have implications for stratospheric chemistry, and that electrons are produced by photoionization of atoms with ionization potentials below 13.6 eV [N1-R2][N1-R3]. This means that solar UV/X-ray photoionization is especially important in the lower atmosphere, where neutral targets are abundant and the energy from solar radiation can efficiently create electrons and ions.

Cosmic rays, by contrast, are a more diffuse and altitude-dependent source. The evidence notes that cosmic-ray ionization rate profiles can peak at different altitudes, with one study reporting peaks between 18 and 22 km altitude, and another showing a peak at 62.5 km under certain conditions [N6-R3][N6-R2]. This highlights that the altitude where ionization is strongest depends on the source: lower-altitude peaks may reflect solar X-ray, proton, and electron precipitation, while higher-altitude peaks may reflect cosmic-ray-induced processes or other altitude-specific chemistry [N4-F1][N6-R3]. The evidence also emphasizes that electron attachment and transport reduce depth-integrated ionization, so even if primary ionization is strong, the net ionization rate depends on how many electrons are retained [N5-R3][N4-F2].

## 2) How solar activity affects ionization through cosmic rays and energetic particles

Solar activity affects stratospheric ionization mainly by modulating cosmic-ray flux and by changing the role of solar wind and energetic particles. The evidence is clear that solar cycle variations are reflected in cosmic-ray intensities, with galactic and anomalous cosmic rays encountering an outward-moving solar wind, and that observed 11- and 22-year cycles in cosmic-ray intensities are discussed in relation to solar activity cycles [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Another source states that solar activity affects cloud formation by allowing more cosmic rays to penetrate during low solar activity, which is consistent with the general understanding that lower solar activity weakens heliospheric modulation of cosmic rays [N2-R5]. This means that during solar minimum, cosmic-ray flux is higher, while during solar maximum, it is lower, and so cosmic-ray-driven ionization is stronger at low solar activity and weaker at high solar activity [N2-R3][N2-R4].

Solar wind and energetic particles also affect ionization differently depending on solar phase. During solar maximum, the solar wind is stronger, which can both enhance ionization through direct solar radiation and reduce cosmic-ray flux by shielding the heliosphere [N2-R4]. The evidence also links solar protons and energetic particles to ionization in the mesosphere and stratosphere, indicating that solar wind-driven particle precipitation is an important contributor, especially during active solar periods [N4-F1]. Thus, solar maximum tends to increase ionization through solar energetic particle events, while solar minimum increases cosmic-ray flux and thus indirect ionization via cosmic rays [N2-R3][N2-R4].

## 3) How solar activity effects differ across altitude and latitude

The effects of solar activity are not uniform across altitude and latitude because ionization sources and loss processes vary with height and magnetic geometry. The evidence on stratospheric ionization by solar X-rays, solar protons, and radiation belt electrons shows that ionization profiles are evaluated at different altitudes and that particle transport simulations are used to quantify altitude-dependent ionization rates [N4-F1]. The cited cosmic-ray ionization study also notes that ionization rate profiles can peak at different altitudes, with one example peaking between 18 and 22 km [N6-R3]. At higher latitudes, auroral and polar particle precipitation becomes more important, as the evidence on geomagnetic storms and auroral precipitation indicates that particle precipitation is a major source of ionospheric storms and that magnetic field geometry controls particle paths [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The evidence further notes that auroral precipitation and electron fluxes can influence ionization at different altitudes, and that particle precipitation can shift lower latitude during geomagnetic disturbances [N3-R4].

This means that solar activity effects are altitude-dependent because different ionization sources dominate at different heights, and they are latitudinally dependent because cosmic rays and auroral particles follow heliospheric and magnetic-field pathways [N2-R1][N2-R2][N4-F1][N6-R3]. The evidence also shows that geomagnetic latitude determines where particles are accelerated and where they precipitate, which explains why auroral zone and polar regions show stronger ionization [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

## 4) Why auroral zone and polar regions show stronger ionization

Auroral zone and polar regions show stronger ionization because they receive stronger particle fluxes, especially from auroral electrons and precipitating protons. The evidence directly states that auroral precipitation and particle precipitation are important sources of ionospheric storms, and that auroral particle precipitation is part of a coupled electrodynamical system involving field-aligned currents and precipitating particles [N3-R2][N3-R3]. The auroral zone and polar regions are especially significant because energetic protons and electrons can precipitate into the atmosphere, increasing ionization there [N3-R5][N4-F1]. This explains why these regions are not uniform in ionization strength: particle precipitation is not spread evenly across latitude, and auroral activity concentrates fluxes into the polar and auroral latitudes [N3-R2][N3-R4].

Magnetic-field geometry controls where those particles precipitate because the evidence notes that field-aligned currents and precipitating particles are electrodynamically coupled, and that auroral precipitation is tied to the structure of the magnetic field [N3-R3]. The evidence also emphasizes that particle precipitation is the result of active geomagnetic activity, reinforcing the idea that geomagnetic latitude is a key driver of ionization strength [N3-R2]. The cited study on geomagnetic storms and atmosphere effects describes a “vertical profile” of geomagnetic storm impacts, consistent with the idea that ionization and related effects vary with altitude and latitude [N3-R1].
